title: Who Would Choose to Live at Minus Fifty?
question: Why do people live in Oymyakon?
message: This video tells curious adults that the coldest village on Earth grew around water that would not freeze, not by accident.
angle: Herders stopped at warm springs that stayed open all winter; the stopping place became a village in the 1920s and 1930s, a Soviet weather station made it famous, and today the cold itself draws visitors.

scenes.role: hook: con số đời sống + Wob muốn chuyển tới
scenes.narration: Eyelashes freeze here. Cars stay running all night. And around five hundred people live here on purpose. Wob has already packed a suitcase.

scenes.role: lời hứa: câu hỏi lạ hơn, mở vòng phán quyết
scenes.narration: This is Oymyakon, a village in the Sakha Republic, in the far east of Russia. It is often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth. Most videos about it ask how people survive here. That is a fair question. But it skips a stranger one. Why is there a village here at all? Somebody chose this spot, in the middle of all this. By the end of this video, you will know why. And Wob will decide whether to unpack.

shots.cue: Why is there a village here at all

scenes.role: chương 1: kỷ lục và tranh cãi Verkhoyansk
scenes.narration: So just how cold does it get? On the sixth of February, nineteen thirty-three, the weather station here recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That is about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight. So even the number itself comes with an argument. Either way, it is the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost. Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number. Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed. Rival towns. A tenth of a degree. More than a century of arguing. Wob finds this very relatable.

shots.cue: Either way, it is the lowest
Some sources say the two towns

scenes.role: cú lật: Tomtor cũng nhận là Pole of Cold
scenes.narration: There is a second argument, much closer to home. The weather station behind that famous number is not in Oymyakon itself. It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield. Tomtor would like you to know this. Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument. So Wob, who wants to move somewhere truly freezing, now has to choose between the village with the monument and the village with the thermometer. Wob suggests sharing. Nobody is interested. It is very cold outside, and nobody is backing down.

scenes.chapter: Why Is It So Cold Here?
scenes.role: địa lý: áp cao Siberia + thung lũng giữ khí lạnh
scenes.narration: But why is it so cold here to begin with? Oymyakon is not even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it. The cold is a team effort. First, in winter a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space. Second, there is the valley itself. Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor. So the village sits at the bottom of a giant bowl, full of the heaviest, chilliest air around. Wob would like a smaller bowl.

wob.cue: But why is it so cold
Wob would like a smaller bowl

scenes.role: chương 2: nghĩa của tên, suối ấm
scenes.narration: Now the bigger question. In a place this cold, why would anyone stop here at all? Part of the answer is hiding in the name. Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze. Linguists argue about the exact roots, and some sources trace the word to the Even language while others point to Sakha. But the story told about this valley is the same. Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter. And if you move reindeer across a frozen landscape, open water is not a curiosity. It is the whole point. Wob, who has spent this entire trip complaining about frozen water bottles, suddenly understands.

scenes.role: lý do 1: điểm dừng thành làng
scenes.narration: Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys. A stopping place became a regular camp. Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village. So Oymyakon did not appear despite the cold. It appeared because, in the middle of all that cold, there was one thing that refused to freeze. Wob, who has never herded anything in its life, finds this deeply moving. Wob is now looking for the spring. Wob does not find the spring. Wob finds a very surprised reindeer.

shots.cue: the camp grew into a permanent village
So Oymyakon did not appear despite the cold

scenes.role: chương 3: trạm khí tượng, sân bay
scenes.narration: In the Soviet era, the state pushed deep into this region. A weather station was set up. An airfield was built near Tomtor. And the record that made Oymyakon famous came from that station in nineteen thirty-three. In other words, Oymyakon became famous for its cold partly because someone finally put a thermometer there.

shots.cue: A weather station was set up

scenes.role: bối cảnh lịch sử nghiêm túc: Gulag, đường Kolyma (không đùa)
scenes.narration: This was also one of the darkest periods in the region's history. In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold. Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties. Many of them did not survive. The village's story begins with the springs. But the highway that crosses this region was built by people who had no choice.

wob.cue: Many of them did not survive

scenes.narration: So what is daily life like? In January, the average temperature here is around minus forty-six Celsius. In late December the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day. Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets. Yes, even in January. Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting, because a frozen engine may refuse to start at all.

scenes.role: mồi lại: Wob ra ngoài, đổi ý lần 1 (hài)
scenes.narration: Food comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible. Wob decides to test all of this personally. Wob steps outside. Wob does not technically have eyelashes. They freeze anyway. A few minutes later, Wob is back indoors, holding a cup of tea with both hands, quietly reconsidering several life choices.

scenes.role: trường nghỉ vì lạnh (mức C, nói dè dặt)
scenes.narration: Children here are tough, but not unlimited. According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two. The exact cut-off for each age group depends on who you ask. For comparison, plenty of schools elsewhere close for a light dusting of snow. Wob asks whether Oymyakon has snow days. The answer is yes. They are just extremely specific.

scenes.role: chương 5: mùa hè nóng, Wob đổi ý lần 2
scenes.narration: And then, the twist. Oymyakon is not cold all year. Summers are short, but they can be properly warm. By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours. In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That is about ninety-four Fahrenheit. Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth swing that far in a single year. Wob, who packed nothing but fur, is suddenly optimistic again.

scenes.role: chương 6: vì sao giờ vẫn ở, dân số giảm
scenes.narration: So why do people stay now? For many families, this is simply home. Some of the toughest locals are not even human. Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter. A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats. Wob, whose only adaptation is a large backpack, is impressed. Not everyone stays, though. The wider Oymyakonsky district counted around seven thousand seven hundred people in the twenty twenty-one census, down from about ten thousand in twenty ten. Life at the Pole of Cold is a choice that families keep making, or don't, every year.

shots.cue: Life at the Pole of Cold

scenes.role: du lịch giá lạnh: lễ hội, Chyskhaan, marathon
scenes.narration: And the cold itself has become a reason to visit. Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor. Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence. In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here. In the cold. On purpose. A village that grew up around water that wouldn't freeze now welcomes visitors because of everything that does.

scenes.role: phán quyết NOPE + câu hỏi bình luận
scenes.narration: So, would Wob move here? The springs are lovely. The summers are a genuine surprise. And the people of Oymyakon have built a real home in one of the hardest places on the planet. But Wob lasted a few minutes outside and spent most of them looking for warm water. The verdict is NOPE. This is a place for people who grew up with it, or who truly, deeply love winter: silence, clear skies, and a summer that feels earned. Wob is unpacking. Slowly. With gloves on. So, be honest. How long would you last out there?

shots.cue: The summers are a genuine surprise

verdict.label: NOPE
verdict.reason: Wob lasted a few minutes outside and spent most of them looking for warm water.

claims.quote: Eyelashes freeze here. Cars stay running all night.
claims.statement: In winter in Oymyakon, Russia, temperatures are cold enough that people's eyelashes freeze outdoors and residents often leave car engines running for long periods so they will restart.

claims.quote: And around five hundred people live here on purpose.
claims.statement: The village of Oymyakon in the Sakha Republic, Russia, has roughly 500 permanent residents (462 in the 2010 Russian census).

claims.quote: It is often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth.
claims.statement: Oymyakon is often described as the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth.

claims.quote: On the sixth of February, nineteen thirty-three, the weather station here recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That is about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight.
claims.statement: On 6 February 1933 the weather station at Oymyakon, Russia, recorded about minus 68 degrees Celsius (about minus 90 Fahrenheit); Guinness World Records lists the value as minus 67.7 C and the World Meteorological Organization lists minus 67.8 C.

claims.quote: Either way, it is the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's 1933 reading is the lowest recorded temperature for a permanently inhabited place, though Verkhoyansk has a comparable reading and some sources treat the record as shared.

claims.quote: Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number.
claims.statement: Verkhoyansk, Russia, northwest of Oymyakon, recorded a temperature of about minus 67.7 to minus 67.8 degrees Celsius in February 1892.

claims.quote: Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed.
claims.statement: Some sources (for example Guinness World Records) describe Oymyakon and Verkhoyansk as sharing the record low for an inhabited place, while the World Meteorological Organization lists only Oymyakon and treats the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed.

claims.quote: It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield.
claims.statement: The weather station associated with Oymyakon's temperature records is located in a valley between the villages of Oymyakon and Tomtor, near the airfield at Tomtor, rather than in Oymyakon village itself.

claims.quote: Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument.
claims.statement: Some sources argue that the nearby village of Tomtor, where the record was measured, is the real Pole of Cold, while the official Pole of Cold monument stands in Oymyakon.

claims.quote: Oymyakon is not even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it.
claims.statement: Oymyakon (about 63.5 degrees north) lies south of the Arctic Circle (about 66.5 degrees north).

claims.quote: First, in winter a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space.
claims.statement: In winter, the Siberian High, a semi-permanent area of high pressure, sits over eastern Siberia, bringing clear, dry, stable air that allows strong radiative cooling of the ground around Oymyakon.

claims.quote: Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's valley setting traps dense cold air near the valley floor (a temperature inversion), and studies have found that in winter the surrounding mountain slopes can be much warmer than the valley floor.

claims.quote: Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze.
claims.statement: The name Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning unfrozen or non-freezing water.

claims.quote: some sources trace the word to the Even language while others point to Sakha
claims.statement: Sources disagree on the origin of the name Oymyakon: some derive it from the Even language (for example the word kheium), others from the Sakha (Yakut) language.

claims.quote: Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter.
claims.statement: There are warm or thermal springs near Oymyakon whose water does not freeze in winter.

claims.quote: Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys.
claims.statement: Reindeer herders historically stopped at the springs near Oymyakon to water their reindeer and rest.

claims.quote: Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village.
claims.statement: Over time, the herders' stopping place at Oymyakon grew into a permanent village.

claims.quote: A weather station was set up. An airfield was built near Tomtor.
claims.statement: During the Soviet period a weather station was established near Oymyakon and an airfield was built near the village of Tomtor.

claims.quote: the record that made Oymyakon famous came from that station in nineteen thirty-three
claims.statement: Oymyakon's fame as the coldest inhabited place rests largely on the minus 67.7 degrees Celsius reading taken at its weather station in 1933.

claims.quote: In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold.
claims.statement: In the 1930s the Soviet Union built a network of Gulag forced labour camps across the Kolyma region of north-eastern Siberia, largely for gold mining.

claims.quote: Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties.
claims.statement: Construction of the Kolyma Highway began in the early 1930s using Gulag prisoner labour, and forced labour was used on it into the 1950s.

claims.quote: Many of them did not survive.
claims.statement: Many of the prisoners who built the Kolyma Highway died during its construction.

claims.quote: In January, the average temperature here is around minus forty-six Celsius.
claims.statement: The average January temperature at Oymyakon is around minus 46 degrees Celsius.

claims.quote: In late December the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day.
claims.statement: Around the December solstice, Oymyakon gets roughly four and a half hours of daylight per day.

claims.quote: Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets.
claims.statement: Oymyakon sits on permafrost, which makes conventional water pipes difficult to maintain, and many homes there use outdoor toilets.

claims.quote: Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting
claims.statement: In Oymyakon, cars are often left running for long periods or warmed with a fire before starting, because engines may not start in extreme cold.

claims.quote: Food comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible.
claims.statement: The diet in Oymyakon relies heavily on meat and fish, fish is sold frozen in winter, and farming is very difficult because of the frozen ground.

claims.quote: According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two.
claims.statement: In the Oymyakonsky district of Yakutia, classes for younger schoolchildren are cancelled when the temperature falls to around minus 52 degrees Celsius; exact thresholds for different ages vary between reports.

claims.quote: By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours.
claims.statement: From around mid-June to the solstice, daylight at Oymyakon lasts more than 20 hours per day.

claims.quote: In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That is about ninety-four Fahrenheit.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's weather station recorded a high of 34.6 degrees Celsius (about 94 Fahrenheit) in July 2010.

claims.quote: Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth swing that far in a single year.
claims.statement: The difference between Oymyakon's record low (minus 67.7 C) and record high (34.6 C) is about 102 degrees Celsius, one of the largest temperature ranges of any place on Earth.

claims.quote: Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter.
claims.statement: Yakutian horses in the Sakha Republic live outdoors all year round, including through the winter.

claims.quote: A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats.
claims.statement: A 2015 genomic study (Librado et al., PNAS) found that Yakutian horses descend from domestic horses brought to the region a few centuries ago and adapted to the subarctic cold very quickly, with compact bodies and very hairy winter coats.

claims.quote: The wider Oymyakonsky district counted around seven thousand seven hundred people in the twenty twenty-one census, down from about ten thousand in twenty ten.
claims.statement: The Oymyakonsky district of the Sakha Republic had a population of 7,730 in the 2021 Russian census, down from 10,109 in the 2010 census.

claims.quote: Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor.
claims.statement: A festival called Pole of Cold (Journey to the Pole of Cold) is held each spring in the Oymyakonsky district, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor.

claims.quote: Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence.
claims.statement: Chyskhaan, the Lord of Cold in Sakha (Yakut) tradition, is a central figure of the Pole of Cold festival and has an ice residence associated with him.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here.
claims.statement: A marathon called Pole of Cold - Oymyakon was held in the Oymyakon area in 2025.
